In brief

Joyce sprinkles some Hebrew into Bloom's thought and speech, but he does not give him (and perhaps did not himself know) Yiddish expressions. The only exception comes in Lestrygonians when Bloom thinks that Denis Breen is "Meshuggah. Off his chump." Both the Yiddish and the English expression mean crazy, eccentric, mad, off one's rocker, out of one's senses.

At more length

"Meshuggah," or meshuge or a dozen other similar spellings, is a Yiddish word derived from the ancient Hebrew m'shugá. The root sense is wandering, being led astray—hence deranged, driven mad. Perhaps Joyce did not know anything about the etymology, but it applies particularly well to Breen, who not only seems to have been driven out of his right mind by the insulting postcard but who manifests his derangement by wandering all over Dublin looking for a solicitor to file an action on his behalf.

One would expect Bloom to have learned some Yiddish words from his central European Jewish father, but if so he does not use them much. Joyce probably learned some Hebrew from Ettore Schmitz (Italo Svevo), but Schmitz was a financially successful assimilated Jew who may not have trafficked much in Yiddish expressions. Meshuggah is one of those Yiddish words (schlemiel, schmaltz, mensch, chutzpah, klutz, schmooze, nosh, schlep) that have entered into English usage so thoroughly as not to require italics or dictionary definitions. It is also a great word for casual putdowns and broad jokes. One such joke concerns Sigmund Freud leading a group of interns around a psychiatric ward. After visiting each patient he records a diagnosis—hysteria, paranoid schizophrenia, whatever the joke-teller likes. But some patients prompt Freud to write simply, TM. At the third such mystery a student asks, What is TM? the doctor replies with a mixture of cultivated-academic-man German and good-Jewish-boy Yiddish: "Total meshuggah."

John Hunt 2026
